nameStory: The creek heelsplitter gets its unusual name from its remarkably thin shell that can split easily along its edges, like a cracked heel. The 'creek' part refers to its preference for smaller waterways rather than large rivers or lakes. Early naturalists thought these delicate shells looked like they could split your heel if you stepped on one barefoot!
description: The creek heelsplitter is a freshwater mussel that lives buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of streams and creeks. Like all mussels, it's a bivalve - meaning it has two hinged shells that protect its soft body inside. These mollusks are filter feeders that spend their lives quietly cleaning the water by straining out tiny particles of food. They typically grow to about 3-4 inches long and have an elongated, somewhat flattened shell shape.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Elongated and compressed (flattened from side to side), feeling thin and delicate when handled, unlike the chunky thickness of many other mussels

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth exterior with fine growth lines that feel like gentle ridges under your fingertip, lacking the heavy ridges or bumps of other mussel species

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Yellowish-brown to dark brown exterior, often with darker rays radiating from the hinge area, while the interior is typically pearly white or bluish

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Medium-sized mussel reaching 3-4 inches in length, fitting comfortably in an adult's palm when fully grown

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found buried in sand or fine gravel in flowing water, often with just the back edge visible above the substrate

habitat: Creek heelsplitters live in clean, flowing streams and small rivers throughout New England, particularly in areas with sandy or fine gravel bottoms. They prefer well-oxygenated water and are often found in the St. Lawrence River drainage system. Look for them in shallow riffles and runs where the current keeps sediment from building up too heavily.

seasonality.spring: Most active during spring months when water temperatures rise and they begin filter feeding more actively. This is when you're most likely to see them partially exposed above the sediment.
seasonality.summer: Continue active feeding throughout summer, though they may burrow deeper during very hot weather or low water conditions. Their filtering activity helps keep streams clear.
seasonality.fall: Begin preparing for winter by burrowing deeper into the substrate. Their feeding activity slows as water temperatures drop and food particles become less abundant.
seasonality.winter: Remain buried in the streambed sediment in a dormant state, with very little activity. They can survive under ice as long as some water flow continues to provide oxygen.

funFact: Creek heelsplitters are living water purifiers - a single mussel can filter up to 10 gallons of water per day, removing bacteria, algae, and pollutants, making them nature's biological water treatment plants that have been cleaning New England's streams for thousands of years!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the flutedshell, its close relative in the same genus, but the creek heelsplitter lacks the distinctive ridged 'flutes' and is noticeably more compressed and thinner. Remember: if it feels delicate and thin like it might crack easily, it's likely the heelsplitter.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that freshwater mussels like the creek heelsplitter are completely different from the marine mussels you might eat at a restaurant. These freshwater species are native mollusks that play crucial ecological roles and should never be harvested or moved from their natural habitat.
compareHints: The creek heelsplitter differs from its relative the flutedshell by being much more compressed and lacking the prominent ridges or 'flutes' that give its cousin its name. While both species have smooth shells compared to other mussel families, the creek heelsplitter feels noticeably thinner and more delicate when handled. Both prefer similar flowing water habitats, but the creek heelsplitter tends to be found in smaller streams.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The flutedshell differs from its relative the creek heelsplitter by having those diagnostic fluted ridges, while the heelsplitter has a smoother shell surface.
